title: Stuck in a Rut
whyItMatters: Silver-Bridge 2D Event Simulation: With coordinates up to 10⁹ and N ≤ 1000 cows, hour-by-hour grid simulation is impossible! Instead, sorting East-facing cows by y-coordinate and North-facing cows by x-coordinate processes potential intersections in exact topological order — letting you resolve both stopping times AND transitive blame counts in clean O(N²) time.

paragraphs: Farmer John has recently expanded the size of his farm, so from the perspective of his cows it is effectively now infinite in size! The cows think of the grazing area of the farm as an infinite 2D grid of square "cells", each filled with delicious grass. Each of Farmer John's N cows (1 ≤ N ≤ 1000) starts out in a different cell; some start facing north, and some start facing east.

Every hour, every cow either: (1) Stops (and remains stopped from that point on) if the grass in her current cell was already eaten by another cow, OR (2) Eats all the grass in her current cell and moves one cell forward according to the direction she faces. If two cows move onto the same grassy cell in the same move, they share the cell and continue moving in their respective directions in the next hour.

If cow b stops in a cell that cow a originally ate, we say that cow a stopped cow b. Moreover, if cow a stopped cow b and cow b stopped cow c, we say that cow a also stopped cow c (that is, the "stopping" relationship is transitive). Please compute the amount of blame assigned to each cow — that is, the total number of cows she stopped.
inputFormat: The first line of input contains N (1 ≤ N ≤ 1000).

Each of the next N lines describes a cow's starting location: a character 'N' (north, (x, y) → (x, y + 1)) or 'E' (east, (x, y) → (x + 1, y)) followed by two integers x and y (0 ≤ x, y ≤ 10⁹). All x-coordinates are distinct, and all y-coordinates are distinct.
outputFormat: Print N lines of output. Line i should give the blame assigned to the i-th cow in the input.

sampleExplanation.title: Sample Analysis
sampleExplanation.detail: Cow 3 stops Cow 2 (blame[3] = 1). Cow 5 stops Cow 6 (blame[5] = 1), and then Cow 4 stops Cow 5 — so by transitivity Cow 4 stops both Cow 5 and Cow 6 (blame[4] = 2)!
sampleExplanation.steps: Cow 3 → Cow 2  |  Cow 4 → Cow 5 → Cow 6  ⇒  blame = [0, 0, 1, 2, 1, 0]

hints.title: Which Pairs of Cows Can Possibly Intersect?
hints.body: Since all x-coordinates are distinct and all y-coordinates are distinct, two East cows never intersect and two North cows never intersect! An East cow e = (xₑ, yₑ) and a North cow n = (xₙ, yₙ) can ONLY cross at cell (xₙ, yₑ), and only when xₑ < xₙ and yₙ < yₑ.

hints.title: Sort East Cows by y↑ and North Cows by x↑!
hints.body: Sort East cows by increasing yₑ (bottom to top), and North cows by increasing xₙ (left to right). Loop over each East cow e (lowest yₑ first), and inside loop over each North cow n (smallest xₙ first). Why is this order magical? Because when you reach an unstopped pair (e, n) with xₑ < xₙ and yₙ < yₑ, every earlier obstacle that could have stopped e (at x < xₙ) or stopped n (at y < yₑ) has ALREADY been processed!

hints.title: Compare Arrival Times & Accumulate Transitive Blame
hints.body: For an unstopped pair (e, n) with xₑ < xₙ and yₙ < yₑ, let dx = xₙ − xₑ and dy = yₑ − yₙ. If dx < dy, e arrives first and stops n: mark stopped[n] = true and add blame[e] += 1 + blame[n] (since n stops at yₑ, all cows n ever stopped had y < yₑ and are ALREADY counted in blame[n]!). If dx > dy, n arrives first and stops e: mark stopped[e] = true, add blame[n] += 1 + blame[e], and break out of the inner loop! (If dx == dy, tie — neither stops!)

editorial.summary: Separate East-facing cows (sorted by ascending y) and North-facing cows (sorted by ascending x). Scanning East cows bottom-to-top and North cows left-to-right visits every valid crossing (xₙ, yₑ) in topological order: whichever cow arrives strictly later stops, and its finalized blame subtree (1 + blame[stopped]) is added directly to the stopper.

solutions.python:
import sys

def solve():
    tokens = sys.stdin.read().split()
    n = int(tokens[0])
    east = []
    north = []
    idx = 1
    for i in range(n):
        d = tokens[idx]
        x = int(tokens[idx + 1])
        y = int(tokens[idx + 2])
        idx += 3
        if d == 'E':
            east.append((x, y, i))
        else:
            north.append((x, y, i))

    east.sort(key=lambda c: c[1])
    north.sort(key=lambda c: c[0])

    stopped = [False] * n
    blame = [0] * n

    for xe, ye, ie in east:
        for xn, yn, in_idx in north:
            if stopped[in_idx]:
                continue
            if xe < xn and yn < ye:
                dx = xn - xe
                dy = ye - yn
                if dx < dy:
                    stopped[in_idx] = True
                    blame[ie] += 1 + blame[in_idx]
                elif dx > dy:
                    stopped[ie] = True
                    blame[in_idx] += 1 + blame[ie]
                    break

    print("\n".join(map(str, blame)))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    solve()
